sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Use this example as the model for the guided set below.

items.prompt: A population has 500 students. Student A takes a random sample of 10. Student B takes a random sample of 50. Both use proper random selection. Whose sample is more likely to give an estimate closer to the true population value?

steps: Both samples are random, so neither is biased by the selection method.
A larger random sample generally has less variability between repeated samples.
Student B's sample of 50 is larger than Student A's sample of 10, so it is more likely to be closer to the true population value.
workedSolution.answer: Student B's sample of 50, because larger random samples tend to produce more consistent, accurate estimates.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A student surveys 24 students at Lincoln Middle School using a convenience sample of her classmates only and records the results. Is it valid to generalize this result to all 480 students at Lincoln Middle School?
choices: Yes, because the sample size is large enough regardless of how it was chosen.
No, because the sample was not randomly selected, so it may not represent the population.
No, because samples can never be generalized to a population.
Yes, because the sample was selected randomly, so it is likely representative of the population.

items.prompt: A sample of 5 values is: 12, 13, 21, 10, 15. What is the median of this data set?
A data set has 5 values: 19, 18, 17, 25, 21. What is the new mean if an outlier of 60 is added to the data set, making 6 values in all?
A data set is: 5, 19, 23, 25, 3, with a mean of 15. What is the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of this data set?
Two data sets have means of 60 and 77. Their mean absolute deviation (MAD) is 7. Express the difference between the means as a multiple of the MAD.
choices: 3 3/7 times the MAD
2 3/7 times the MAD
5 3/7 times the MAD
4 6/7 times the MAD

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Sample A: 20, 18, 18, 19, 55. Sample B: 40, 27, 35, 45, 28. Based on the means, which sample tends to have greater values?
choices: Both samples have the same mean.
Sample B, with a mean of 35 compared to 26.
Sample B, with a mean of 26 compared to 35.
Sample A, with a mean of 26 compared to 35.

items.prompt: Sample A: 34, 22, 33, 18, 37. Sample B: 30, 31, 30, 28, 28. Based on the range of each sample, which sample is more consistent (less variable)?
choices: Sample B, with a range of 3 compared to 19.
Sample B, with a range of 19 compared to 3.
Sample A, with a range of 19 compared to 3.
Both samples have the same range.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to know about all 1785 shoppers at a grocery store. She randomly selects 16 of them to survey. What is the sample in this situation?
choices: All 1785 shoppers at a grocery store
The researcher's own estimate
Only the first 16 shoppers at a grocery store on a list
The 16 randomly selected shoppers at a grocery store

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Mastery check. Work without help, then stop and hand this section in.

items.prompt: A student surveys the 36 commuters on a train line sitting closest to her. Is this sampling method likely to produce a representative sample?
choices: Yes, likely representative — every member had a fair, known chance of being chosen.
No, likely not representative, because the population is too large.
Yes, likely representative, because the sample size is large enough.
No, likely not representative — the method favors certain members over others.

items.prompt: In a random sample of 12 visitors to a science museum, 8 preferred a new park design. Based on this sample, about how many of the 48 visitors to a science museum would you expect to prefer a new park design?
